title: What is toil, and how do you reduce it in a DevOps/SRE team?
shortTitle: What is toil, and how do you reduce it in a DevOps/SRE team

s1_definition.profdef: Toil is operational work that is manual, repetitive, automatable, tactical rather than strategic, devoid of enduring value, and that scales linearly with the size of the service. It is the kind of work that keeps a service running but produces nothing lasting — the same task done again and again by hand. Reducing toil means identifying it, measuring the time it consumes, and systematically eliminating it through automation, self-service tooling, better defaults, and fixing the root causes that generate it, so engineers spend their time on engineering that produces durable improvements.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, imagine a clerk who every single morning manually unlocks each of the five hundred ATMs one by one, types the same code into each, and writes the result in a ledger by hand. It takes three hours, it has to be redone every day, it grows worse as the bank opens more ATMs, and at the end of it nothing permanent has been built — tomorrow the exact same three hours are needed again. That is toil. Reducing it means building a system that unlocks all five hundred ATMs with one button and records the results automatically, so the clerk's three daily hours are freed to work on something that actually improves the bank, like designing a faster transfer flow for Rajesh and Priya.
s1_definition.oneliner: Toil is manual, repetitive, automatable work that scales with the service and leaves nothing behind — you reduce it by measuring it and engineering it away so people do lasting work instead.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Toil is operational work that is manual, repetitive, automatable, tactical rather than strategic, devoid of enduring value, and that scales linearly with the size of the service. It is the kind of work that keeps a service running but produces nothing lasting — the same task done again and again by hand. Reducing toil means identifying it, measuring the time it consumes, and systematically eliminating it through automation, self-service tooling, better defaults, and fixing the root causes that generate it, so engineers spend their time on engineering that produces durable improvements.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, imagine a clerk who every single morning manually unlocks each of the five hundred ATMs one by one, types the same code into each, and writes the result in a ledger by hand. It takes three hours, it has to be redone every day, it grows worse as the bank opens more ATMs, and at the end of it nothing permanent has been built — tomorrow the exact same three hours are needed again. That is toil. Reducing it means building a system that unlocks all five hundred ATMs with one button and records the results automatically, so the clerk's three daily hours are freed to work on something that actually improves the bank, like designing a faster transfer flow for Rajesh and Priya.

**One line to remember:** Toil is manual, repetitive, automatable work that scales with the service and leaves nothing behind — you reduce it by measuring it and engineering it away so people do lasting work instead.

sections.s2_technical:
The precise definition of toil from site reliability engineering has several characteristics, and work is toil to the degree it matches them. It is manual, meaning a human performs the steps by hand. It is repetitive, done over and over rather than once. It is automatable, meaning a machine could do it just as well — if a task genuinely requires human judgement every time, it is not toil. It is tactical and interrupt-driven rather than strategic and planned. It has no enduring value, meaning after it is done the service is in the same state as before, not improved. And it scales linearly with service growth, so as you add more servers, more customers, or more traffic, the toil grows in proportion rather than staying flat. Classic examples are manually restarting a stuck service, hand-applying the same configuration change across many hosts, manually provisioning accounts, responding to the same alert with the same fix each time, and manually running a release checklist.

Toil is not the same as overhead. Overhead is administrative work like meetings, email, and expense reports — necessary but separate. Toil specifically is operational work tied to running the service. Some toil is unavoidable and even healthy in small doses, because touching the system keeps engineers familiar with it, but the SRE guideline is to keep toil below about fifty percent of an engineer's time so the rest goes to engineering projects that reduce future toil. When toil creeps above that, the team is on a treadmill: all its time goes to keeping the lights on and none to improvement, and the toil only grows as the service grows, eventually overwhelming the team.

Reducing toil starts with measuring it. You cannot manage what you do not measure, so you track how much time the team spends on toil, often by categorising on-call and operational tickets. Once you see where the hours go, you attack the biggest sources. The primary weapon is automation — turning a manual runbook into a script, then into a self-healing system. A manual service restart becomes an automated health check that restarts the service, which becomes a system designed not to get stuck in the first place. Self-service tooling removes toil by letting the people who need something do it themselves safely, instead of filing a ticket for an engineer — for example a self-service portal to provision a test database rather than a human doing it. Better defaults and platforms remove whole classes of toil, such as an internal platform that gives every team standardised deployment, monitoring, and rollback without each team reinventing it.

Crucially, you also fix root causes rather than just automating the symptom. If an alert fires every night and you keep applying the same fix, the best outcome is not a script that applies the fix faster but a change that stops the alert from firing at all. A senior nuance: automating a bad process just makes the bad process faster, so before automating you ask whether the task should exist at all. You also prioritise toil reduction like any engineering work, with a backlog and an owner, because toil reduction that is only done when there is spare time never happens — there is never spare time on a team drowning in toil. And you watch for toil that is hidden inside heroics, where one person quietly absorbs huge manual effort and masks the problem until they burn out or leave.
sections.s3_banking:
The National Bank of India's SRE team is drowning. Every night the transfer service accumulates stuck transactions, and an on-call engineer manually logs in, finds the stuck transfers for customers like Rajesh and Priya, and reprocesses them one by one. The team wants to measure this toil and automate it away.

Problem 1 — The team must first identify and measure the toil: how many minutes per day the manual reprocessing consumes, and confirm it has the toil characteristics — manual, repetitive, automatable, no enduring value, and growing with transaction volume.

Problem 2 — The team automates the task: a scheduled job that detects stuck transfers and reprocesses them automatically, turning a nightly manual chore into zero human minutes.

Problem 3 — The team goes one step further and fixes the root cause so transfers stop getting stuck in the first place, which is better than merely automating the cleanup.

Our runnable Java simulation models a `ToilTracker` that scores a task against the toil characteristics and measures time spent, and an `Automation` that replaces the manual task, with the demo comparing engineer-minutes before and after automation and after the root-cause fix. Classes: `ToilTask`, `ToilTracker`, `Automation`, and a `ToilDemo` main.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: the nightly stuck-transfer reprocessing task, which takes forty-five minutes each night across thirty nights a month, and exhibits all five toil characteristics; plus a counter-example quarterly capacity review that needs human judgement.

Step 1: The tracker assesses the nightly task. It scores five out of five on the toil characteristics — manual, repetitive, automatable, no enduring value, and scaling with transaction volume. It consumes thirteen hundred fifty minutes a month, which is over thirteen percent of an engineer's month, so it is flagged as high toil to prioritise.

Step 2: Because it is clearly toil consuming significant time, the team automates the cleanup. A scheduled job now detects and reprocesses stuck transfers automatically, dropping the engineer's time on this task from thirteen hundred fifty minutes a month to zero.

Step 3: The team goes further and fixes the root cause by adding idempotent retries and timeouts so transfers stop getting stuck in the first place. This eliminates the toil entirely rather than just automating the symptom, which is the superior outcome.

Step 4: The tracker assesses the counter-example, the quarterly capacity review. It scores low because it is not repetitive, not automatable, and needs human judgement each time, so it is correctly classified as not toil and kept as real engineering work.

Step 5: The journey shows the full discipline: measure the toil, confirm it against the characteristics, automate it away, and best of all remove its root cause, while being careful not to mislabel genuine judgement work as toil.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Toil is operational work that is manual, repetitive, automatable, tactical rather than strategic, devoid of enduring value, and that scales linearly with the size of the service. The defining test is that after you finish a piece of toil, the service is in exactly the same state as before — nothing lasting was built — and tomorrow the same work is needed again, growing worse as the service grows. Classic examples are manually restarting a stuck service, hand-applying the same config across many hosts, and responding to the same alert with the same fix every night. Toil is different from overhead like meetings and email; toil is specifically operational work tied to running the service.

A little toil is healthy because it keeps engineers familiar with the system, but the guideline is to keep it below about fifty percent of an engineer's time. Above that, the team is on a treadmill where all its time goes to keeping the lights on and none to improvement, and because toil grows with the service it eventually overwhelms the team. So the first step in reducing it is measuring it — categorising on-call and operational tickets to see where the hours actually go — because you cannot manage what you do not measure.

Then I attack the biggest sources, in order. Automation is the primary weapon: a manual runbook becomes a script, then a self-healing system. Self-service tooling removes toil by letting people safely do things themselves instead of filing a ticket for an engineer. Platforms and better defaults remove whole classes of toil at once. But the most important discipline is to fix root causes rather than automate symptoms, because automating a bad process just makes the bad process faster. In my project at the National Bank of India, an on-call engineer spent forty-five minutes every single night manually reprocessing stuck transfers for customers like Rajesh and Priya — thirteen hundred fifty minutes a month, scoring every toil characteristic. We first automated the reprocessing with a scheduled job, taking that to zero engineer-minutes, and then we went further and added idempotent retries and timeouts so transfers stopped getting stuck at all, eliminating the toil instead of merely hiding it. The principle I always state is measure the toil, keep it under control, automate relentlessly, and whenever possible remove the root cause so the toil never has to exist.
